shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're born in Birmingham in 1801, in a back room that smells of brass filings and boiled cabbage.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your father takes one look at you and asks the midwife whether the next one will be a boy.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You are an hour old, and you have already disappointed the family business.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The business is buckles. Your father is a journeyman in a workshop where forty men hammer

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: tiny bits of metal for customers who will never know their names.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your mother polishes the finished ones at the kitchen table,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: by candlelight, for a few pence a dozen. Between them they earn enough to eat. Not one penny more.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: by candlelight, for a few pence a dozen. Between them they earn enough to eat. Not one penny more.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Birmingham is a loud town, and everything in it is for sale.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Buttons, buckles, guns, a day of your labour.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The loudest place of all is the Bull Ring, the market at the heart of the town.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Cattle on one side, cabbages on the other, and a crowd shouting prices over both.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You'll spend a lot of time there. Remember it.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You'll spend a lot of time there. Remember it.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: At home, you learn the rules early.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The truth is, English law has a word for what happens to a woman at her wedding.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It's called coverture. A wife, the law says, doesn't exist on her own.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: She is "covered" by her husband, like a table under a cloth.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Her wages are his. Her furniture is his. Her children are his.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: She can't sign a contract or bring a case to court without him.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: In short, a wife is a person who is legally permitted to be present.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your mother puts it more simply. "Marry carefully," she says. "You only do it once."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: She means that literally.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: There is exactly one legal way out of an English marriage, and it isn't built for people like you.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: First, a church court must agree that the couple may live apart.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Then the husband must sue his wife's lover in a second court.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Only after that can Parliament pass a private law, just for that one couple.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Three separate cases, years of waiting, and a bill of hundreds of pounds, often over a thousand.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your father is lucky to earn a pound in a good week.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: For families like yours, divorce isn't forbidden. It's just something that happens to dukes.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Nobody mentions any of this as a warning. They mention it the way they mention the weather.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Nobody mentions any of this as a warning. They mention it the way they mention the weather.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're six when you first hear the words. You're sitting on the back step, shelling peas,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: when a neighbour leans over the fence and tells your mother about a woman three streets away.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "She went for four shillings," the neighbour says.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your mother clicks her tongue. "Cheap."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You assume they mean a hen. A bad hen, probably.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: By eight, you're working. Your mother takes you to the buckle shop and sits you

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: at a bench to sort the little metal tongues by size,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: twelve hours a day, for a few pennies a week.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The room is hot, and the air tastes of metal.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your fingers learn to find a bent tongue by touch,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and by ten you can sort a whole tray in the dark.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Nobody calls it a skill. Nobody pays for it, either.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The first time you're paid, you hold the coins for exactly as long as the walk home.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Then you hand them to your father. After all, they were never going to be yours.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're eleven when you finally ask what the four shillings were for.

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: You ask the woman herself. Her name is Peg, she sells pies from her front window,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and she laughs so hard that she has to sit down on an upturned bucket.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "Not a hen, love," she says. "Me."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Her window smells of hot pastry and onions. A queue of hungry men forms outside it every noon,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and she says they taught her everything she knows about haggling.

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: Peg tells it like the best night out of her life.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Her first husband was a nail-maker with a face like a boiled ham and about as much conversation.

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: Peg loved a cooper named Alf, and had done for two years.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Nobody in her position could afford Parliament, so they did what people in her position did.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: They held a Smithfield bargain.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The name comes from London's great meat market, and it fits.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The bellman went round the streets that morning, ringing and shouting that a wife would be sold at noon.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Her husband tied a rope of straw round her neck and led her to the Bull Ring.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He offered her to the crowd like a heifer. Alf, who had known the plan for a week, bid four shillings.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Nobody dared bid higher. The husband took the money, signed a scrap of paper,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and the three of them walked to the pub and drank to it.

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: "Nobody cried," Peg says. "Except the nail-maker, when he saw the bill for the ale."

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: The truth is, Peg isn't unusual. The custom has no legal force at all.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Magistrates don't love it, but they mostly shrug,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and one historian has confirmed more than two hundred cases across England,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: with plenty more that never reached a newspaper. In the eyes of the street, it's as good as a church,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: because everyone in sight has agreed to treat it that way.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "Was it real?" you ask.

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: "Real as anything," says Peg. "The law doesn't care. The street does."

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: Then she gets serious, which, from Peg, is alarming.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "It only works if all three say yes. Him, the buyer, and her.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: If the woman isn't willing, it's not a bargain.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It's a man dragging his wife through a market on a rope."

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: You ask what happens then. Peg hands you a pie. "Eat that."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You eat the pie. It's a good pie.

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: What you don't realize is that Peg has just told you the only rule that will ever matter.

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: What you don't realize is that Peg has just told you the only rule that will ever matter.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Years pass as you turn nineteen, and you marry Ned.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned is an ostler at a coaching inn near the market, the Hen and Chickens.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Of course it's called the Hen and Chickens. You never tell anyone why you laugh.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned is easy to like. He sings. He lifts you off the ground when he's happy.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Everyone agrees he's wonderful with animals, and you take that as a compliment.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your father arranges the match the way he arranges everything: over a pint, in about four minutes.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned has a steady wage and a roof.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The vicar at St Martin's, the church that stands over the Bull Ring,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: asks if you will take this man. You say "I will."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It isn't a question so much as a line you were given.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: For a few years, it's genuinely good. You rent a room above a chandler's shop.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: On Saturdays Ned takes you to the market and buys you a ha'penny gingerbread,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and you eat it slowly so that it lasts the whole walk home.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: In 1822, you have a daughter. In 1825, a son.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned sings to both of them in the same cheerful voice he uses on the horses.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: In the quiet of the night you think, this is it.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: This is what the rules were for.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Married life, you discover, runs on a timetable.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're up at five to fetch water from the pump and light the fire.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: You make Ned's breakfast, then the children's,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: then you scrub whatever the day has made dirty, which is everything.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: In the evening you mend, and cook, and listen to him describe his day.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Nobody calls any of this work. They call it being a wife.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Still, you keep a tin under the floorboard, with a few coppers in it.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You aren't sure why. Peg's voice, perhaps. Legally the tin is his too.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: But it makes you feel better.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're twenty-nine when things start to fall apart.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned argues with the landlord over a bill and is dismissed from the Hen and Chickens.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It was the landlord's fault, he tells you. For some reason, it's always somebody else's fault.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: You move to one room. Ned finds evening work at a tavern, serving drinks.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Mostly he drinks them. Instead of complaining, you take in washing.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You stand over copper tubs from dawn, and your hands go red and then grey.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: You earn about six shillings a week, and on Friday night Ned collects it.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: After all, it's his. Every few weeks he finds the tin.

shots.subject: SAM
shots.text: To cover the rent, you take in a lodger. He's a brass-caster in his forties, a widower,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: who speaks about eleven words a week, four of them "thank you".

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He mends your son's boots without being asked. He fixes the broken stair.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He is, you notice, the only man in the house who fixes things.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: What you don't know is that Ned has found someone else.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The barmaid at his tavern is expecting his child.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The whole street knows. Nobody tells you. Nobody ever tells the wife.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: The truth is, Ned has a problem he can't solve.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He can't afford a lawyer. He can't afford Parliament.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He can't afford two households. But he remembers Peg, and a rope of straw.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He can't afford two households. But he remembers Peg, and a rope of straw.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: One Monday evening, you're carrying a basket of damp sheets

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: through the Bull Ring when the bellman starts to ring.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "Oyez," he shouts, and the crowd gives him half an ear.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: On Thursday, at noon, a man will sell his wife by auction to the highest bidder.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He says the man's name. It's Ned's.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The wife isn't named. She doesn't need to be.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Halfway across the square, the sheets in your arms become very heavy.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Immediately, you walk home.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned is at the table with a tankard, whispering to himself.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He has a speech. You can see his lips moving.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You'd expect shouting. It isn't like that.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned tells you, quietly, that he isn't a cruel man,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and the strange thing is, he isn't.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He's a man with a barmaid, a baby on the way,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and a law with one door, and that door was built for dukes.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "Peg did it," he says. "It worked for Peg."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He adds that Peg fetched four shillings and a quart of ale,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and that he'd happily settle for the ale.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "Peg said yes," you say.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He looks at you like a puzzle that's missing a piece.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Then he tells you the children will stay with him.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: This isn't a negotiation.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The law, he points out, is on his side, so he doesn't have to negotiate.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He's right. A father in England has every right over his children.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: A mother has the right to be informed that she's leaving.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You nod. You say nothing at all.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Nobody asks what you think, and, to be fair to Ned, he never claimed otherwise.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Thursday comes.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The Bull Ring at noon is ordinary and loud. Cattle low in their pens.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Stallholders shout about turnips. Somebody, somewhere, is selling pins.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The whole square smells of dung, wet straw and frying onions.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: And in the middle, where a crowd has formed the way crowds do when someone is about to be humiliated,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: there is a clear space, and it's meant for you.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned ties the rope of straw round your neck himself.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He does it the way he ties up a horse at the Hen and Chickens.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Quick. Gentle. Without looking. He's very good with animals.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He leads you into the middle by the loose end.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: People step back to let you through. A child laughs.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Another child asks what you did. The straw scratches your neck.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It's a small, stupid discomfort,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and for some reason it's the only thing in the world you can concentrate on.

shots.subject: DAUGHTER
shots.text: Your daughter is in the crowd, twelve years old, holding your son's hand.

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: He's nine. Peg is there too, shoving through the elbows with her hand over her mouth.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: When she reaches the front, she shouts something at Ned that you can't print.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He pretends not to hear her. It's the only thing he has ever pretended well.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned clears his throat. He's been practising. "Gentlemen," he says.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "I offer you my wife, with all her perfections and imperfections."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You wonder what he thinks the imperfections are. He lists three. One is your cooking.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It isn't an original speech.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Two years earlier, in Carlisle, a farmer made almost exactly the same one.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He asked fifty shillings. He settled for twenty, plus a Newfoundland dog.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He asked fifty shillings. He settled for twenty, plus a Newfoundland dog.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned asks ten shillings. Nobody says anything.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The silence is the loudest thing in the Bull Ring.

shots.subject: DROVER
shots.text: Then a drover at the back,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: a cattle man who knows exactly what animals are worth, calls out, "Two."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Two shillings. For a person. The crowd laughs, and you hear every voice.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're worth, to the town of Birmingham, less than a decent dinner.

shots.subject: DROVER
shots.text: "Four," says the drover. He's looking at you the way he looks at stock.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your hands. Your shoulders. Your teeth, almost.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You stare past him, at the church where you were married.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "Six."

shots.subject: SAM
shots.text: You know the voice. It's the lodger.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He's pushed to the front of the crowd, brass dust still on his hands, breathing hard.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He has never said so many words in public.

shots.subject: DROVER
shots.text: "Seven," says the drover, shrugging.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "Nine."

shots.subject: DROVER
shots.text: Silence. The drover weighs it up.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Seven shillings, it seems, is the price of a woman.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Nine is the price of a mistake. He shakes his head and turns away.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: "Nine shillings," says Ned. "Going once. Going twice."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The bellman rings.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned signs a scrap of paper. The lodger counts out nine shillings, then pays for the bell,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: then buys a round of drinks for the whole crowd.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: This is the custom. The buyer pays for the wife, and for the party.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned unties the straw from your neck and lets it drop onto the cobbles.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Then he shakes your new owner's hand,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and the three of you go to the pub and sit at one table, because that is also the custom.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Everyone laughs. You are the only one who doesn't.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your daughter doesn't wave. She's twelve.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: She has already decided something about you, and it will take years to find out what.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The truth is, none of it counts.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The sale has no legal force, and a court, if anyone asked, would tell you so.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: In the years ahead, courts will increasingly do just that.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You've been sold, and you're still married. Both things are true.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're the only person in the Bull Ring who finds that strange.

shots.subject: SAM
shots.text: That night, the lodger walks you back to his attic above the brass foundry, three streets away.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He carries your basket of damp sheets and doesn't say a word.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He gives you the bed and takes the floor. In the morning, he has made tea, badly.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It's the first morning in fourteen years when nobody tells you what you are.

shots.subject: PEG
shots.text: On Sunday, Peg comes by with a pie. She doesn't say anything clever.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: She sits with you for an hour, and when she goes, she leaves the pie.

shots.subject: SAM
shots.text: You stay. His name, it turns out, is Sam.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: For the first time in your life, you keep what you earn.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He never asks for your wages.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He puts a few coins on the table every Friday and says it's for the house.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He eats what you cook and says it's fine, which,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: after fourteen years of Ned, sounds like poetry.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The neighbours whisper. You can't marry Sam in church, because you already have a husband,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and a second wedding is a crime. The stallholders in the Bull Ring start calling you "Nine Bob."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Not unkindly, mostly. It's what you cost, in the only currency anyone has ever offered.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: In 1839, Parliament finally lets some mothers ask a judge for custody of their small children.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Only mothers with a spotless reputation. Only children under seven.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Your children are seventeen and fourteen. And you have a reputation.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: You're forty when Ned turns up at your door.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The barmaid has left him, taking the baby and most of the furniture.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He's thinner. He's sober enough to be polite.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He hasn't come to take you back. He's come for your wages.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Turns out, he's been to see a clerk.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He's been told, correctly, what you've never been able to forget.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The sale meant nothing. You're still his wife.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Everything you earn is his. He doesn't need to prove that he sold you.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He only needs to prove that he married you.

shots.subject: SAM
shots.text: Immediately, you want to fight. Sam stays quiet.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Then he points out, gently,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: that in a court somebody will ask what exactly happened at the Bull Ring that Thursday,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: and nobody in the room will be able to answer it safely.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: So you pay. A shilling a week, every Friday,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: folded in a scrap of paper and handed over at the corner by the church.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Over ten years, it comes to nearly sixty times what you were sold for.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You were bought for nine shillings, and you pay for it for a decade.

shots.subject: NED
shots.text: Ned gets his money twice.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Ned dies in the workhouse infirmary, owing money to three taverns.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: A parish clerk sends a letter addressed to "the widow."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You read it standing at the sink.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're fifty years old, and for the first time since you were nineteen,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: you are legally nobody's wife.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You don't cry. For a while you don't feel anything at all.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Then you sit down on the kitchen floor and feel everything at once, for about an hour,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: until Sam finds you and sits down on the floor next to you without saying a word.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: A few months later, he asks if you'd like to be married.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He asks in the kitchen, with both hands wrapped round a tin mug, as if the question might spill.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: And then he does something nobody has done in fifty-one years.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: He waits for the answer.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You take a full minute. He waits the whole time.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You say yes. It's the first yes you've ever given that was entirely yours.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're married at St Martin's, the same church, the same Bull Ring below the steps.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The vicar asks if you will have this man.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The words are the same as the first time.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The answer is not.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: At the back, in the last pew,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: sits a woman of thirty with a stern, familiar face.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: She doesn't speak. She doesn't come forward.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: But she stays until the end.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It's about all she can give, and for now it's enough.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It's about all she can give, and for now it's enough.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: What you never learn is how long the custom outlived you.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: In 1857, Parliament opened a divorce court.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: It was cheaper than an Act of Parliament, which isn't the same as cheap, and it wasn't fair.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: A husband needed to prove one thing. A wife needed to prove more.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Wife sales faded, but they didn't vanish. As late as 1913,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: a woman told a court that her husband had sold her to a workmate for a pound.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: The custom lived on in the imagination, too.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: In 1886, Thomas Hardy opened a novel, The Mayor of Casterbridge,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: with a drunk man selling his wife at a country fair for five guineas.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: Readers recognised it at once. Hardy didn't have to invent a thing.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You're sixty-eight, sitting on a back step in Birmingham, shelling peas.

shots.subject: GRANDDAUGHTER
shots.text: Your granddaughter, who is six, comes out of the house with a puzzled face.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: A woman at the market, she tells you,

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: said that someone once went for nine shillings.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: She asks what it means.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: You think about it for a long time.

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "A hen, love," you say. "A very good hen."

shots.subject: YOU
shots.text: "A hen, love," you say. "A very good hen."

events.text: Remember the market. It's going to be important. Unfortunately.
Smithfield bargain. Divorce, but with livestock.
Spoiler: he did not ask Peg how it went for the wife.
IT'S HOW PEOPLE LIKE US DO IT.
Eighteen years. Nine shillings. Still no refund.
